start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start beefsteak seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant date. In the Southeast and Gulf region that is roughly mid-February for the Georgia interior (zone 8) and two to three weeks earlier toward the warmer Gulf-coastal zone 9 end. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: the last week of March or first week or two of April
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set beefsteak transplants out in spring once frost danger passes. UGA gives late March into the first half of April for middle Georgia (zone 8); the warmer zone 9 end runs two to three weeks earlier. Beefsteak is large-fruited and slower to mature than cherry types, so time it to set fruit before peak summer heat arrives. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Beefsteak begins ripening roughly three months after transplanting (about 75 to 90 days to maturity, longer than cherry types). The spring crop comes in from late June, just as the summer heat begins to shut fruit set down. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop ends as summer heat sets in. Large-fruited tomatoes are more sensitive to high day and night temperatures than cherry types, so blossom drop and fruit-set failure begin earlier for beefsteak, by about June. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

start_indoors.label: primary

plant_out.label: primary

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out as the worst summer heat eases so plants establish and produce into the cooler fall. The warmer zone 9 end runs about two weeks later, into early August. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary

harvest_end.label: primary

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit-set failure is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Large-fruited beefsteak is more heat-sensitive than cherry types (which are heat resistant), so its summer pause is wider, running across June through August rather than the single midsummer month a cherry holds. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

after.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf area you can grow beefsteak tomatoes twice a year, once in spring and again in fall, with a summer break in between when it gets too hot for the plants to set fruit. Big beefsteak tomatoes handle the heat less well than small cherry tomatoes, so their summer break is longer, running through most of the summer. Plant your spring crop early enough to pick before the heat, then plant again in late summer once the worst heat passes for a fall crop.
after.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf region runs two beefsteak seasons, spring and fall, split by a summer heat window when high day and night temperatures cause blossom drop and fruit set fails. Large-fruited beefsteak is more heat-sensitive than cherry types, so its summer pause is wider, spanning roughly June through August rather than a single midsummer month. Beefsteak also needs 75 to 90 days to mature, longer than cherry, so time the spring crop to set fruit before peak heat and set the fall crop out promptly once the heat eases (UGA gives a July 20 fall deadline for middle Georgia so the crop beats frost). The warmer zone 9 end plants the spring crop earlier and the fall crop later than the zone 8 interior. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

after.region_notes_beginner: In California's low desert (Imperial and Coachella valleys) you grow beefsteak tomatoes in the cool months, not the summer. Plant the main crop from December through March so it makes fruit before the extreme heat, and plant a second crop in early fall (around September) once the worst heat breaks. Summer (June through August) is simply too hot for any tomato to set fruit, so the plants rest then.
after.region_notes_seasoned: California's desert valleys (Imperial, Coachella) grow beefsteak on an inverted, two-window calendar driven by extreme summer heat. The main crop is set out across the cool season, December through March, to mature and set fruit before summer; a second fall crop goes out in early fall (about September) as the heat breaks and produces into the mild winter. June through August is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: complete blossom drop for every tomato type, not narrowed for beefsteak, which is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry. Confirm local frost for the winter harvest tail. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the spring beefsteak crop out in late March to early April, after the high-desert last frost (Las Cruces sits in Chihuahuan high desert, last frost about March 19). The Master Gardener chart's early-March transplant is an experienced-grower date; reconcile to the local last frost for a first crop. (NMSU Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardener Las Cruces planting chart)

harvest_start.label: primary

harvest_end.label: primary

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors in mid-June, about six weeks before the mid-July transplant the Master Gardener chart specifies. (Dona Ana County Master Gardener Las Cruces planting chart; NMSU Circular 457)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall beefsteak crop out in mid-July to early August (the Las Cruces chart transplants the fall tomato crop in mid-July). For large-fruited beefsteak this fall crop is marginal in this short-autumn high desert: a 75-90 day plant set in mid-July only just matures before the November frost, and fruit set through the hot July-August transplant period is poor. (Dona Ana County Master Gardener Las Cruces planting chart; NMSU Circular 457)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about three months after the mid-July transplant, bringing fruit in from roughly mid-October. (NMSU Circular 457)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop is harvested up to the high-desert first frost (about November 12); the productive tail is short for slow-maturing beefsteak. (NMSU Circular 457)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: July is the peak fruit-set-failure month: high-desert day temperatures exceed 95 degrees F and large-fruited beefsteak drops blossoms and fails to set, though arid nights recover into the 60s. Set failure continues through August for large-fruited types; the fall crop is transplanted into this window (mid-July) and establishes through the back of the heat, so July reads as the fall-planting month while fruit set itself is poor through August. after.region_notes_seasoned: The southern high desert (Las Cruces, Mesilla Valley; Chihuahuan high desert, zone 8) runs two beefsteak windows split by peak summer heat. Set the spring crop out in late March to early April, after the local last frost (about March 19), so it sets fruit before July. A fall crop can be transplanted in mid-July per the Dona Ana County Master Gardener chart, but for large-fruited beefsteak this is marginal: fruit set is poor once day temperatures exceed 95 °F through July and August, and a 75-90 day plant only just matures before the November frost (about November 12). Favor fast-maturing, heat-tolerant cultivars for the fall attempt. The fall window and two-window structure rest on the single Las Cruces Master Gardener chart, a regional source; the spring dates are anchored to the high-desert frost data with NOAA cross-check. 11.calendar_basis: Beefsteak tomato can be planted YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no documented summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. UNLIKE cherry (which CTAHR treats as cleanly heat resistant), CTAHR's Field Tomato Production Guidelines specifically warn that large-fruited varieties set fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights (optimum fruit set 60-70 deg-F). This is a fruit-set-QUALITY caveat, disclosed in the seasoned region_note, not an absolute no-sow month, so the year-round structure holds (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted; HGV-5 documents no exclusion month). Hawaii's dominant challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally bred cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, N-series) and cultural practice. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason; year_round:true makes the all-active calendar machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

after.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii's tropical lowlands you can plant beefsteak tomatoes any month of the year; there is no cold winter and no planting season to wait for. The catch is that big beefsteak tomatoes do not set fruit well in the warm tropical nights, so they do best at cooler elevations and in the cooler parts of the year, and you will have the most luck with heat-tolerant or locally bred varieties. The bigger day-to-day challenges are disease, bugs, and heavy rain.
after.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical zone 11 grows beefsteak year-round: CTAHR gives a year-round planting capability for most of the islands contingent on adapted varieties, with no winter cold pause and no documented summer no-sow exclusion. The important caveat for beefsteak specifically is fruit-set quality, not timing: CTAHR's field production guidance notes that large-fruited varieties are sensitive to high night temperatures and set fruit poorly in the warm lowland (optimum set 60-70 °F), unlike heat-resistant cherry types. Favor cooler-elevation siting, the cooler part of the year, and heat-tolerant or locally bred wilt-resistant cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, the N-series). The dominant production challenges here are disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant varieties and cultural practice rather than a seasonal stop. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)
